turns: I have an interview for the Restaurant Manager role at Sweetgreen on Thursday. prep me
replies:
Good — we’ll prep to a tight, practice-ready set. I assumed you want a 60‑second "tell me about yourself", three STAR stories (team win, hard problem, failure) with measurable results, three behavioral practice questions to answer aloud, two concise why-this-role/company lines, and two smart questions to ask them. If you want a different tone (more formal or more casual), say so.

Tell me your name and one short fact I should use in the answers (current job title or most recent role) and I’ll save it; otherwise I’ll leave [your current role] in brackets for you to insert.

1) 60‑second "Tell me about yourself" (fill bracket)
"Hi, I’m [Your Name]. I’ve spent the last [X years] managing fast‑paced restaurant teams, most recently as [your current role] where I led a crew of [#] through daily operations and drove guest experience improvements. I focus on coaching teams to hit operational metrics — labor, speed of service, and food quality — while cutting waste and improving profitability. For example, I implemented a prep and scheduling change that reduced labor hours by [Y]% and improved on‑time orders by [Z]%. I enjoy building positive, repeatable processes and mentoring shift leaders; Sweetgreen’s focus on thoughtful operations and sustainable growth is why I’m excited about this manager role. I’m looking forward
to bringing my people‑first leadership and operational discipline to your store."

2) Three STAR stories (short, repeatable; replace bracketed facts)
A. Team win — boosting guest satisfaction and throughput
- Situation: During a busy summer, customer wait times and complaints rose at my store.
- Task: I needed to lower wait times and raise guest satisfaction without increasing labor costs.
- Action: I introduced a cross‑training rotation for front and back stations, redesigned the point‑of‑sale flow to batch orders by station, and ran a two‑week coaching blitz with shift leads on upsell + speed techniques.
- Result (numbered): Within four weeks average ticket time dropped from [A] to [B] minutes (≈[X]% improvement), and our guest satisfaction scores rose by [Y] points; we maintained the same labor spend.

B. Hard problem — inventory waste and cost
- Situation: We had excessive food waste that was cutting into margins.
- Task: Reduce waste while keeping menu availability.
- Action: I audited daily usage, changed ordering par levels, implemented FIFO prep logs, and trained staff on portion control and labeling.
- Result: Waste costs fell by [X]%, saving ~$[Y] per month and improving our contribution margin by [Z] points.
C. Failure and learning
- Situation: I rolled out a new shift‑handoff checklist to reduce mistakes but the first week still had repeated errors and low adoption.
- Task: Fix adoption and make the checklist actually useful.
- Action: I held short feedback sessions with crews, simplified items (from 12 steps to 6), added a two‑minute verbal handoff ritual, and recognized teams for clean handoffs.
- Result & lesson: Errors decreased by [X]% in two weeks and adoption stayed high. I learned to test with frontline staff first and iterate quickly — change needs to be simple and owned by the team.
3) Three behavioral practice questions — say answers out loud, 2 minutes each
- "Tell me about a time you managed a conflict between two team members. What did you do and what was the outcome?"
- "Describe how you ensured operational standards and cash/food safety compliance on a busy day."
- "Give an example of when you had to coach someone who wasn’t meeting expectations. How did you handle it and what happened?"

I’ll score your answers if you want a mock; say “mock me for Restaurant Manager at Sweetgreen” and I’ll ask the first question now.
4) Two one‑line answers: Why this role / Why Sweetgreen
- Why this role: "I want this Restaurant Manager role because I enjoy balancing people leadership with operational problem‑solving — building teams that deliver consistent guest experience while improving store performance."
- Why Sweetgreen: "Sweetgreen’s commitment to fresh, sustainable food and scalable operations matches my values and experience running efficient, guest‑first restaurants; I want to lead a store that combines high standards with a purpose‑driven brand."
5) Two questions to ask them (smart, show leadership + curiosity)
- "What are the top three priorities for this store in the next three months, and how does the manager own them?"
- "How do you measure manager success here, and what support or development opportunities are available for people who want to grow beyond store leadership?"

6) Logistics checklist (ask these now to confirm with recruiter)
- Confirm: interview date/time, time zone, video link or address, and who you’ll meet (names/titles).
- Test tech/location the day before and have a quiet backup place.
Next step: tell me your name and current/most recent job title to insert and save; or say “mock me” and I’ll start the first interview question now. One question for you: what’s your current role title (or type yes if I should keep [your current role])?
